glossary.plain: Reinforced Cement Concrete: concrete with steel bars (sariya) inside. Your flat's skeleton (pillars, beams, slabs) is RCC. Never break or drill big holes into RCC without an engineer's OK.
A vertical RCC post that carries the building's weight down to the ground. Never cut or chip it. In Room 1 there is a 9" pillar at the north-west corner.
A horizontal RCC member that runs between pillars just under the ceiling, often showing as a 'drop' in the ceiling. Carries the slab. Never cut it.
The flat RCC plate that forms your ceiling and the floor of the flat above. About 5–6" thick.
Most walls between pillars are just 'filler' walls made of red bricks or AAC blocks, then plastered. 9" for outer walls, 4.5" for inner ones. You can cut these for switches and pipes (not RCC).
A light, large grey building block used instead of red bricks. Easier to cut, insulates better.

In Room 1's south wall, one 7'3" long part sticks 3'4" into the room, so that part of the wall is 3'4" deep instead of normal thickness. It's solid (not a cupboard). Such thick blocks usually wrap a pillar, a shaft for pipes/wires, or the building's structure — ask the builder before cutting into it. The designs use its face for a study desk / dresser.
A 12–15 mm layer of cement and sand spread on bricks to make walls flat. Builders usually hand over walls already plastered (often with one coat of white putty/paint).
An opening is the hole left in a wall for a door or window. A lintel is the small concrete beam over the opening that carries the wall above.

White paste (cement or acrylic based) spread in 2 thin coats (about 1–1.5 mm) on plaster and sanded smooth. It fills pores and small cracks so paint looks smooth. Used only indoors, on walls and ceiling — not waterproof, so never on outside walls. e.g. Birla White WallCare, JK WallMaxx (about ₹30–45 per kg).
A first thin coat that makes paint stick and use less paint. Goes on after putty and before the colour coats (water-based interior wall primer).

Normal water-based wall paint, 2 coats over primer. Three grades (Asian Paints example, 2026 prices for 20 L): economy Tractor Emulsion ~₹212/L, standard Apcolite Premium ~₹437/L, luxury Royale ~₹764/L. Costlier grades are more washable and smoother. Berger, Nerolac and Dulux have similar ranges.
The cheapest chalky wall paint. Marks easily and can't be washed; mostly avoided in bedrooms now.
A soft, cloudy-looking lime-based wall finish. Gives a hand-made textured look. Used on the accent wall in Options A and C.

One wall painted or panelled differently from the others to make it the room's focus, usually the wall behind the bed. In Option D it's the east (bed) wall painted terracotta, the other walls warm white.
A warm brownish-orange, the colour of baked clay pots (matka / kulhad). Calm and earthy; pairs well with white, indigo, cane and wood.
Deep blue from the indigo plant, classic in Indian block-print textiles. Used for Option D's cotton curtains.
Greige = grey + beige (DEFAULT's floor). Sage = soft grey-green (DEFAULT's headboard and curtains). Teal = deep blue-green (Option C's accent wall).
Boards fixed on a wall (fluted, slatted, fabric or cane) for looks and a bit of sound softening. Costs much more than paint.
Plaster of Paris. Used for smooth ceiling finishing, cornices and older-style false ceilings. Gypsum board has mostly replaced POP false ceilings.

A second ceiling hung below the concrete slab using steel channels and gypsum boards. Hides wires, gives space for hidden (cove) lights and recessed downlights. A 'band' or 'peripheral' false ceiling covers only the edges of the room.
12.5 mm white board (Gyproc etc.) screwed to a steel frame to make a false ceiling or partition. Joints are taped, puttied and painted, so it looks like a normal ceiling.
A hidden LED strip tucked in a groove of the false ceiling (or on a pelmet), so you see a soft glow on the ceiling but not the light itself.
A box or board above the curtains that hides the curtain rod or track. In Option D it's a laminated plywood box with an LED strip on top.
A 3–4" strip at the bottom of the walls (tile, wood or aluminium) that protects the paint from mops and feet.

The most common Indian floor today. Made from clay, quartz, feldspar and silica, pressed and fired at about 1,200 °C, so it becomes dense and glass-like: hard, low water absorption, doesn't stain easily. Cheaper and easier to keep than marble. GVT/PGVT = glazed with a printed design (can look like marble, wood or terrazzo). Brands: Kajaria, Somany, Johnson, Nitco.

Indian Patent Stone: a smooth grey cement-concrete floor. Some builders hand over flats with IPS or a rough cement screed so owners can choose tiles. It works, but it's dusty and cold-looking — most people tile over it.
A denser, premium kind of vitrified tile, often in big slabs (1200×1200 mm or more). Used in Option B.
Natural stone (e.g. Makrana white). Beautiful but porous: it stains, needs polishing and costs more. None of the designs use marble, to keep cost and upkeep down.
Hard natural stone, very durable. Used for window sills and door thresholds (black granite) in these designs, not for the whole floor.
A green-grey natural stone from Rajasthan, cheap, tough and cool underfoot. 'Leather finish' = matte textured surface. Used in Option C's balcony.
A floor with chips of stone set in cement and polished. The options use 'terrazzo-look' tiles (vitrified tiles printed to look like terrazzo).
Vitrified tile printed and textured like wooden planks. Looks warm, but you can mop it like tile. Used in Option A.
The filler in the gaps between tiles. Epoxy grout is stain-proof and colour-matched; cement grout is cheaper but darkens over time.
What the tile sits on: a 1:4 cement-sand bed about 40–50 mm thick, or a thin layer of tile adhesive on an already-level floor.
The stone strip at the bottom of a doorway. At the balcony it also steps down and slopes away so rainwater doesn't come in.
Outdoor tile with a rough surface so it isn't slippery when wet. R11 is a slip-resistance rating.
A chemical coating under balcony and bathroom floors so water doesn't leak to the flat below. Needs a slope (fall) towards the drain.
A flat woven cotton or jute rug (Panipat, Jaipur). Cheap, washable, very Indian.
Madhubani: folk painting from Bihar (Option D's framed print). Moodha: a round cane stool. Jaali: a carved lattice screen (Option C).
Thin wooden sheets glued in layers into an 18 mm board. MR = moisture resistant (fine for dry rooms), BWR/BWP = boiling-water resistant/proof (for damp areas, costlier).
High Density High Moisture Resistance board: a pressed fibre board that's harder and cheaper than good plywood and handles humidity well. Popular for wardrobes now.
Cheaper pressed-wood boards. MDF is smooth (good for carving/flutes); particle board is the cheapest, used in ready-made furniture and 'engineered wood'.
The box/body of a wardrobe or cabinet (sides, back, shelves), without the doors.
Carpenter's word for a cupboard door.
The storage box above the wardrobe, up to the ceiling, for suitcases and quilts.
A 0.8–1 mm printed plastic sheet glued on the board (wood-grain, white, colours). Tough, easy to clean and the most economical finish.
A real-wood slice (about 0.5 mm) glued on the board, then polished with PU. Looks like real wood, costs more than laminate.
Premium door finishes: PU is a paint-like polish, acrylic is a glossy sheet, lacquered glass is back-painted glass. Costlier than laminate.
A hinge with a small damper so the door closes gently instead of banging. Hettich / Hafele / Ebco are common brands.
The recessed base under a wardrobe or bed so you can mop under the front and your toes don't hit it.
The common, economical aluminium window/door section in India (27 mm series). Slides on tracks. Good value; slimmer 'system' windows cost more.
Plastic (vinyl) window frames with steel inside. Seals well against dust, noise and rain; white is the standard colour. Used in Option A.
Panels move sideways on 2 or 3 tracks. 3-track lets you have 2 glass panels + 1 mosquito-mesh panel. Doesn't swing into the room, so nothing gets in its way.
A window that opens on hinges like a door (inward or outward). Seals better than sliding. Inward ones need space in front.
A European casement that can tilt at the top for air or swing fully inward to clean. Used in Option B.
Panels fold like an accordion and stack at one side, opening almost the whole width. Used in Option C's balcony.
Glass heat-treated to be about 5× stronger; if it breaks it shatters into small blunt pieces. Standard for doors.
Two glass sheets with a plastic film between. If it cracks, it stays in place, so it can replace a grill.
Glass with a thin coating that keeps out heat from the sun. Keeps rooms cooler; costs more.
A fine net panel or pleated screen so you can keep the window/door open without insects.
Metal bars outside the window glass for safety. 'Invisible grill' = thin steel cables, used in Option B.
The ledge at the bottom of a window. Inside it's often granite; outside it slopes and has a drip groove so rain drips off instead of running down the wall.
A small round ceiling light pointing down. 'Recessed' ones sit inside a false ceiling; 'surface' ones are screwed onto a plain ceiling (Option D).
A flexible tape of small LEDs (sold per metre) that needs a 'driver' (power adapter). Used for cove, pelmet, wardrobe and headboard glows.
How warm or cool light looks: 2700K is warm yellow (cosy, bedrooms), 3000K warm white, 4000K neutral, 6500K cool blue-white (offices).
A rating that means a light is dust-tight and safe in rain, needed outdoors on the balcony.
A light hanging from the ceiling on a cord.
A ceiling fan with a brushless (BLDC) motor: uses about 28–35 W instead of 70–75 W for an old fan, runs quietly and usually comes with a remote. Costs a bit more but pays back in electricity.
A desk whose height changes (by motor or crank) so you can work standing or sitting. Good ones hold their height steadily and have memory buttons for your two heights.
A cushioned rubber / foam mat to stand on at a standing desk; it makes long standing much easier on the feet and knees.

Getting ready for an AC before painting: a separate 16 A power point near where the indoor unit will go, and a pipe hole (sleeve) through the outer wall for the copper pipes and drain. Doing it now means no broken paint later.
A board full of small holes; hooks and small shelves clip in anywhere, so you can rearrange bags, headphones and tools without drilling again.

A thin, smooth, white plaster (6–12 mm) applied straight onto concrete or brick instead of sand-cement plaster. Sets in hours, doesn't crack as easily, and is ready for putty and paint. Used on bare RCC ceilings.
A shallow wall cabinet whose door is a mirror: storage and a full-length mirror in the same wall space.
A false ceiling only along the walls, usually 1.5–2 ft wide, so the middle keeps the full height. Cheaper than a full false ceiling and still hides the wiring for the downlights.
Galvanised (rust-proof) steel sections that form the frame of a gypsum false ceiling. They hang from the slab on rods and anchor bolts.
A steel bolt that expands inside a drilled hole in concrete. Used to hang the false-ceiling frame and to fix a fan hook into a slab that has none.
Wrapping an existing beam in gypsum or wood, often with an LED strip along its sides. A cheap way to make beams look designed.
Paper tape and a filler paste used on gypsum-board joints. Done well, it stops the hairline cracks people complain about.
A small openable square in a false ceiling so the electrician can reach an LED driver or junction box without cutting the ceiling.
Plastic interlocking strips used as a ceiling in bathrooms and balconies. Waterproof and cheap, but the joints show.

DEFAULT.title: Floor
DEFAULT.see: Big matte tiles in a warm light grey-beige (greige), 800×1600 mm (about 2.6' × 5.2').
layers: Cement-sand bed 1:4, about 40–50 mm (levels the floor)
Matte vitrified tile 800×1600 mm, 9 mm, grout in the joints
DEFAULT.simple: It is tile, not marble: glazed vitrified tile that looks calm and doesn't stain. Skirting is cut from the same tile.

DEFAULT.title: Walls (3 walls)
layers: Brick / block wall (built by the builder)
DEFAULT.simple: Normal painted walls: putty makes them smooth, then primer and 2 coats of washable emulsion.
DEFAULT.where: Putty + primer + paint go on the INSIDE faces of all Room 1 walls and on the ceiling (every face you see from inside the room, including the thick wall and the alcove). Outside faces of outer walls get the building's exterior paint (no putty — it isn't waterproof). The balcony walls get exterior-grade paint without putty.
DEFAULT.paint: Standard washable emulsion, low sheen, warm white — e.g. Asian Paints Apcolite Premium (~₹437/L) or Berger/Nerolac equivalent. Ceiling: ceiling-white flat.

DEFAULT.title: Bed wall (east)
DEFAULT.see: A wooden fluted panel behind the bed, 7'8" wide × 8' high, with a thin brass-look strip on top.
layers: 12 mm plywood base screwed to the wall
0.8 mm oak-look laminate wrapped on the strips

DEFAULT.title: Ceiling
DEFAULT.see: A lowered strip (band) around the edges with hidden warm light; the middle stays at the full 10'.
layers: Steel (GI) channels hung from the slab
12.5 mm gypsum board screwed to the channels
DEFAULT.simple: A 'band' false ceiling: gypsum board only along the edges (1'7" wide, 6" deep), with an LED strip hidden in its inner edge and small downlights in it. The centre is the original concrete ceiling, puttied and painted.

DEFAULT.title: Wardrobe
DEFAULT.see: 3-door off-white wardrobe with an oak strip, loft above, 5'3" wide.
layers: Off-white 1 mm laminate on doors, frosty-white inside
Oak-look laminate strip on each door
DEFAULT.simple: Carpenter-made wardrobe that fills the alcove, with drawers, shelves, long hanging and a loft for suitcases.

DEFAULT.title: Window W1
DEFAULT.see: A charcoal aluminium window that slides, with a mosquito-net panel and a grill outside.
layers: 2 glass panels (5 mm toughened) + 1 mesh panel on 3 tracks
DEFAULT.simple: Sliding window: open one glass panel and slide the net over it.

DEFAULT.title: Balcony door
DEFAULT.see: Three big glass panels in a charcoal frame; two slide.
layers: Pleated mosquito net at one side
Black granite threshold with a small step down to the balcony
DEFAULT.simple: Sliding glass door that opens about 7' to the balcony.

DEFAULT.title: Balcony
DEFAULT.see: Outdoor anti-skid tiles, a built-in bench, plants.
layers: Waterproofing on the slab, sloping to the drain
DEFAULT.simple: Non-slippery outdoor tile over waterproofing so rain doesn't leak below.

Wood-look vitrified tile planks 200×1200 mm, grout in the joints

layers: Cement-sand bed 1:4, about 40–50 mm (levels the floor)
Large-format porcelain tile, 1 mm joints, grout in the joints
OPTION_B.simple: Premium big porcelain tiles for a seamless, modern look.

OPTION_B.see: White walls; grey fabric panels behind the bed; concrete-look panel behind the TV.
layers: Brick / block wall (built by the builder)

OPTION_B.where: Putty + primer + paint go on the INSIDE faces of all Room 1 walls and on the ceiling (every face you see from inside the room, including the thick wall and the alcove). 12.5 mm gypsum board screwed to the channels
OPTION_B.simple: A full gypsum false ceiling over the whole room (not just a band).

OPTION_B.title: Wardrobe
OPTION_B.see: Floor-to-ceiling sliding wardrobe in white glass with a mirror.

OPTION_B.title: Window W1
OPTION_B.see: Slim black window: one fixed pane + one tilt-and-turn sash, invisible grill.

OPTION_C.see: Terrazzo-look tiles (speckled), with a brass-coloured strip border 1' from the walls.

Terrazzo-look vitrified tile 600×600, grout in the joints

Teal limewash on the bed wall / warm white emulsion elsewhere
OPTION_C.where: Putty + primer + paint go on the INSIDE faces of all Room 1 walls and on the ceiling (every face you see from inside the room, including the thick wall and the alcove). Outside faces of outer walls get the building's exterior paint (no putty — it isn't waterproof). The balcony walls get exterior-grade paint without putty.

12.5 mm gypsum board screwed to the channels

OPTION_C.see: Teak doors with cane-mesh insets, loft above.

OPTION_C.title: Window W1
OPTION_C.see: Teak-look aluminium casements opening inward, jaali-pattern grill.

OPTION_D.title: Floor
OPTION_D.see: Your existing floor stays (no new tiles). A cotton dhurrie rug adds colour.
layers: Existing floor as handed over by the builder (usually vitrified tile)
OPTION_D.simple: Nothing new is laid. Most new flats are handed over with vitrified tiles; if yours is marble, that's fine too. If it's bare grey cement (IPS), add vitrified tiles like DEFAULT: about ₹30–40k for Room 1.

OPTION_D.title: Walls
OPTION_D.see: Warm-white walls; the bed wall is terracotta (a warm clay-pot brown-orange).
layers: Putty patching only where cracked/uneven (builder's putty kept)
2 coats emulsion: warm white, terracotta on the bed wall
OPTION_D.simple: Just paint: no panels or wallpaper. The builder's existing putty is reused and only repaired, which is why it's cheap.
OPTION_D.where: Putty + primer + paint go on the INSIDE faces of all Room 1 walls and on the ceiling (every face you see from inside the room, including the thick wall and the alcove). Outside faces of outer walls get the building's exterior paint (no putty — it isn't waterproof). The balcony walls get exterior-grade paint without putty.
OPTION_D.paint: Economy emulsion for the white walls — e.g. Asian Paints Tractor Emulsion (~₹212/L). Terracotta accent: same or Apcolite (~₹437/L) tinted to a terracotta / brick-red shade — buy a small sample pot and try a patch first. About 10–12 L in total for 2 coats.

OPTION_D.title: Ceiling
OPTION_D.see: The original flat ceiling, freshly painted white. No false ceiling.
OPTION_D.simple: Nothing is hung from the ceiling. Lights are screwed directly onto it (surface downlights). The soft glow on the balcony side comes from an LED strip on top of the wooden curtain pelmet.

OPTION_D.see: White 3-door wardrobe with a walnut strip and a loft.

Frosty-white 1 mm laminate + walnut laminate strip
OPTION_D.simple: Carpenter-made from economical boards with laminate — the best value finish.

OPTION_D.title: Window W1
OPTION_D.see: White aluminium sliding window with a net panel; plain black grill outside.

OPTION_D.title: Balcony door
OPTION_D.see: White aluminium sliding door, 4 panels; the middle two slide apart.
OPTION_D.simple: About 5' opens in the middle; the end panels stay fixed.

OPTION_D.title: Balcony
OPTION_D.see: Existing balcony floor; folding table and chairs; plants.
layers: Existing floor (check waterproofing: water shouldn't pool)

OPTION_E.title: Floor
OPTION_E.see: The builder's floor stays. A small cotton runner where you step out of bed.
layers: Existing floor as handed over (usually vitrified tile)
OPTION_E.simple: Nothing new is laid. If your floor is bare grey cement (IPS), add vitrified tiles: about ₹30–40k for Room 1.

OPTION_E.title: Walls
OPTION_E.see: Warm off-white walls; the bed wall is a pale sage (a soft grey-green). Just paint.
layers: Putty only where cracked or uneven (builder's putty kept)
2 coats washable emulsion: warm off-white, pale sage on the bed wall
OPTION_E.simple: One paint, two shades. The sage wall costs nothing extra: it's the same paint tinted a different colour. Washable paint matters in a room with a desk: marks wipe off.
OPTION_E.where: Putty + primer + paint go on the INSIDE faces of all Room 1 walls and the ceiling. Outside faces of outer walls get exterior paint (no putty). Balcony walls get exterior-grade paint.
OPTION_E.paint: Mid-range washable emulsion, e.g. Asian Paints Apcolite Premium Emulsion (about ₹270/L), or a Berger / Nerolac equivalent, in matt or low-sheen. Tractor Emulsion is cheaper but marks don't wipe off well. About 10 L for 2 coats of walls + ceiling. Try a sample pot of the sage on the wall first: colours look darker on a big wall.

OPTION_E.title: Ceiling
OPTION_E.see: Now: bare grey concrete (the underside of the roof slab). After: smooth, white, with a fan and 4 flat lights.
layers: RCC roof slab (5" concrete with steel bars)
Fan-hook anchor + thin surface conduits for the light wires
OPTION_E.simple: The 'slab' is your roof: one thick sheet of concrete. From inside you see its underside, which is rough and grey today. Gypsum plaster makes it smooth; then it's painted like a wall. No false ceiling needed. If the terrace is above you, waterproof it and coat it white on top first to keep the room cooler.
OPTION_E.paint: Ceiling-white matt emulsion (e.g. Asian Paints ceiling white or any matt white emulsion), 2 coats over putty and primer.

OPTION_E.title: Wardrobe
OPTION_E.see: White wardrobe with 2 sliding doors and a mirror on the front one; loft above.
layers: 18 mm HDHMR or MR plywood body (carpenter)
5 mm mirror on the front door
OPTION_E.simple: Sliding doors never swing into the entrance. You see half the wardrobe at a time; keep the track clean. Hinged doors are cheaper: switch in ✏️ Customise.

OPTION_E.title: Mirror & pegboard
OPTION_E.see: The mirror is on the wardrobe door; the wall beside the desk holds a pegboard.
layers: 5 mm mirror bonded to the sliding door
OPTION_E.simple: A mirror is most useful where you get dressed. Other choices in ✏️ Customise: a mirror cabinet with storage behind it, or a plain wall mirror.

OPTION_E.see: A desk that goes up and down at the press of a button, with a mirror beside it.

Monitor on a stand, top edge at eye level
OPTION_E.simple: Stand for a while, sit for a while: switch every 30–60 minutes. Elbows at 90° when typing. The mesh chair slides under the desk when you stand.

OPTION_E.title: Window & balcony door
OPTION_E.see: The builder's white aluminium sliders, kept. A folding mosquito mesh is added to the balcony door.
layers: Pleated mosquito mesh on the balcony door
Beige blackout curtains + sheers on SS rods
OPTION_E.simple: Nothing is replaced: cleaning the tracks and oiling the rollers makes old sliders run smoothly again.

OPTION_E.title: Balcony
layers: Tulsi, money plant, snake plant in terracotta pots
OPTION_E.simple: Keep it simple now; add 2 folding chairs later (about ₹2,500).

ui.title: Learn
ui.bare: This model is the bare architecture (no interior design), so there are no finishes to explain. Pick DEFAULT, A, B, C or D under Interior design, or open How homes are built.
ui.lead: You're looking at {d}. Each card says what you'll see, what it's made of (the layers from the structure up to what you touch) and where it goes. Show me flies to it; See pictures opens real photos.
ui.stepslead: The usual order for doing up one room. Each step has to finish before the next, or work gets damaged and redone.
ui.stepsnote: For Option D (budget), steps 2, 5 and 6 are skipped: no civil work, no false ceiling, no new floor.
ui.comparelead: The same room, five ways, in plain words.

svg.wallcap: the wall: bricks, then plaster + putty + paint on the room side

p: Your building stands on an RCC frame (concrete with steel bars): pillars (columns) go up, beams run between them under the ceiling, and a flat slab sits on top — your ceiling and the next flat's floor.
The walls between the pillars are brick or block 'filler' walls. They don't hold the building up, which is why you can cut small grooves in them for wires, but never in pillars, beams or the slab.

ul: Thick ("raised") wall: on the south side, one 7'3" part of the wall is 3'4" deep. It's solid, like a big block, not a cupboard. The designs put the study desk / dresser on its face. Ask the builder what's inside before drilling deep (often a pillar or a pipe/wire shaft).
Alcove: the 5'4" × 3'4" pocket next to it, perfect for a wardrobe, so the wardrobe takes no floor space from the room.
Balcony opening: the whole west side (10'5") opens to the balcony; there's no gate or frame yet, which is why every design adds a glass door.
9" pillar at the north-west corner where the opening ends.

basics.h: 3 · What's on a wall, a floor and a ceiling
stacks: Tile (vitrified) or stone, grout in the joints
notes: Which side gets putty and paint? Only the inside faces of the room's walls and the ceiling. Outside faces of outer walls get exterior paint from the building (putty isn't waterproof, so it's never used outside). The balcony's walls get exterior-grade paint, no putty.

floorpaint.h: What is your floor made of?
p: Under every floor is the concrete slab. On it the mason lays a cement-sand bed (~40–50 mm) to make it level, and on that the tiles or stone, with grout filling the joints. So it's never 'just cement' — unless the builder left an IPS (smooth grey cement) floor for you to tile.

The designs use vitrified tiles, not marble. A vitrified tile is made of clay, quartz, feldspar and silica, pressed and fired at about 1,200 °C until it turns dense and glass-like — hard, hardly absorbs water, doesn't stain. Marble is natural stone: beautiful but porous, needs polishing and costs more.
table: Fired clay-and-glass tile, printed or plain
Whatever the builder laid (usually vitrified tile)
Only if the builder left it — then add tiles

p: Walls and ceiling get the same 4 layers: putty (2 coats) → primer (1 coat) → emulsion paint (2 coats). What changes between designs is the paint grade and colour. Prices below are Asian Paints 20-litre rates (2026); Berger, Nerolac and Dulux have matching ranges at similar prices.
table: Wall putty (Birla White WallCare, JK WallMaxx)
notes: How much? Room 1 has about 590 sq ft of wall + ceiling. A litre of emulsion covers roughly 100–120 sq ft per coat, so 2 coats need about 10–12 litres.

Terracotta accent wall? Terracotta is the warm brown-orange of a clay pot (matka / kulhad). Pick a terracotta or brick-red shade from the shop's colour fan deck, buy a small sample pot and paint a 2'×2' patch first — colours look different on the wall and at night.

steps: Fix the layout, the finishes and the budget first. Changes later cost double.
Breaking / building walls, making openings. Never touch pillars, beams or the slab without an engineer.
Frames go in before the final putty so the edges can be finished neatly.
Wires in pipes (conduits) cut into the brick walls: switch boards, light points, AC point. Done before putty and flooring.
Steel channels + gypsum boards, with holes for downlights and a groove for the cove LED.
Tiles laid on a cement bed; left to set 2–3 days; skirting fixed. Cover it with sheets afterwards.
Walls and ceiling: 2 coats of putty, sanding, primer. Dusty work, so before carpentry is finished.
Wardrobe, loft, study wall, pelmet. Usually 1–2 weeks for one room.
2 coats of colour after the carpentry dust is gone. Touch-ups at the very end.
Lights, switches, fan, LED strips and drivers.
Window glass & mesh shutters, curtain rods, bed, mattress, rugs, plants.
Acid-free cleaning of tiles, remove paint spots, then move in.

OPTION_E: One washable emulsion (Apcolite-class), pale sage bed wall

p: Your real ceiling is the concrete slab. Anything hung below it is a false ceiling. It is a light steel frame with boards screwed to it, with a gap above for wires. You don't have to cover the whole room: a border (peripheral) ceiling covers only a 1.5–2 ft band along the walls.
table: A second ceiling hung below the slab on steel channels
False ceiling only along the walls; the middle stays at full height
A small open lip in the false ceiling with a hidden LED strip that lights the ceiling softly
Small round light set into the false ceiling, pointing down
A thin aluminium strip light, surface-fixed or set in a groove
Galvanised (rust-proof) steel sections that make the frame
12.5 mm white board (Gyproc, USG Boral) screwed to the frame
Plaster of Paris, poured or moulded on a mesh by hand
Wrapping an existing beam in board, often with LED along its sides

Your hall slab is at 10 ft, but two beams hang down to 9 ft. A full false ceiling must pass under the beams, so the whole hall would drop to about 8'8". That makes a big room feel squashed, and it's the most expensive choice.

A 2 ft border sits just under beam level, hides the wiring for the downlights, and its cove LED washes the middle with soft light. The beams then look like part of the design. The middle keeps its full 10 ft.
notes: Too tight on money? Skip the border and just box the two beams with an LED strip along their sides (≈₹17k–36k).

p: Rates are installed prices from Indian cost guides (2025–26, big cities). Local Sheikhpura rates are usually lower, so get 2–3 quotes. My rating is for your flat (hall / bedroom / bath, out of 10).

Designer look, full height in the middle
Cheapest decorative option, uses your beams
Hides everything, hotel look; loses height
Rich and warm; costly, dusty grooves

ceiling.h: Can we do this after plastering? Yes
p: Yes, every ceiling option goes on after plaster. A false ceiling, beam boxing or PVC panels are screwed onto the finished, plastered slab with anchor bolts. Ceiling work normally comes after plaster and wiring, and before the final putty and paint. Your plaster being done is the normal starting point.
What matters is the order of the other jobs:
table: Wiring and AC pipes first, then the ceiling frame, then putty and paint everywhere
Let it cure and dry; boards on damp plaster grow fungus
No wire pipes in the slab
Above the border, wires run in loose pipe, so no cutting. In plain rooms use a neat surface conduit painted ceiling-white, or cut only into the plaster, never into the concrete
No fan hook in the slab
The electrician fixes an anchor-fastener fan hook into the slab (drill 10–12 mm). The fan always hangs from the slab, never from the false ceiling
Ceiling work makes dust and scratches; plan one final touch-up coat after it
Cover the floor with sheets or cardboard; the contractor works on scaffolding
Damp patch or leak on the ceiling
Find and repair the leak (roof, bathroom above, pipe) before covering it, or it will spread under the board

ceiling.h: How a gypsum border is made, step by step
ul: Mark the level line on all walls with a laser (8'11" for your hall).
Perimeter angle: an L-shaped steel strip screwed to the walls on that line.
Hangers: rods from the slab on anchor bolts, holding the GI channels.
Boards: 12.5 mm gypsum screwed on, with the cove lip and the downlight holes cut out.
Joints: paper tape + jointing compound, sanded smooth (this stops cracks).
Finish: putty, primer and paint, at the same time as the walls.
Lights last: LED strip and driver in the cove, downlights in their holes. Leave a small access panel near each driver.
p: About 3–5 working days for a hall your size, plus paint time.

ul: Cheap black (non-galvanised) channels: they rust and stain the board. Ask for GI.
No access panel: when an LED driver fails you have to cut the ceiling open.
Cove too shallow: you see a row of LED dots. Ask for a 5–6 in deep cove and a COB or diffused strip.
Cool-white (6000 K) cove: looks like a shop. Use warm white 3000 K.
Too many downlights: 8 in the hall band is enough; use separate switches for cove, downlights and the main light.
Plain gypsum near bathrooms or the kitchen: use moisture-resistant (green) board or PVC there.
Starting the ceiling before the wiring and the AC pipe are decided.

p: Almost every Indian floor today is vitrified tile: clay and glass powder fired at about 1,200 °C until it hardly soaks up water. The names differ in where the pattern is and how shiny the top is.
table: Softer clay tile; walls and budget floors
Colour pressed 3–4 mm deep; very tough, few designs
Printed design under a glaze; huge choice, not slippery in matt
GVT polished to a mirror shine; marble look, slippery when wet, shows scratches
Same colour through the whole thickness; chips hardly show
Very few joints, luxury look; needs skilled laying
Grey-green natural limestone; outdoor, not slippery
Natural stone, beautiful, stains and needs polishing
notes: Prices are material only from 2025–26 Indian guides; laying adds about ₹15–40 per sq ft, adhesive ₹10–30. Add 18% GST.
links: GVT, PGVT, double-charge, full-body: the difference
Tile prices per sq ft (Orientbell, May 2026)

tiles.h: What we chose, room by room, and why
table: Matt GVT, 600×1200 (2 × 4 ft), warm light shade
Big room: big tiles mean fewer joints and a calmer look. Matt is not slippery and hides footprints; PGVT shines but is slippery and scratches.
Smaller rooms: less cutting and waste; same shade so the flat feels connected.
Safety for parents on wet floors; epoxy grout doesn't turn black or let water through.
Matt wall tile 300×600, up to 7 ft
Full splash height, easy to wipe.
Wall tile 300×600 above the counter (2 ft band) or to 6 ft
Oil and steam wipe off. The band is cheaper; 6 ft (Papa's plan) is easier to keep clean.
Hardest common stone: heat, knives and feet don't hurt it.
Cheap, outdoor-proof, not slippery in rain.
4 inch, cut from the floor tile
Protects the wall from mop water and kicks; matches the floor.
notes: Not chosen: PGVT (slippery, scratches), marble (stains, upkeep), plain ceramic on floors (chips), wooden-look tiles in bathrooms.

p: Out of 5 for your flat. Higher is better (for 'slippery', higher means safer).
notes: If money is tight in the hall, double-charge 600×600 is the tough budget option; full-body is the 'never shows a chip' upgrade.

p: Papa's 'ग्रेनाइट 3' most likely means the usual three granite jobs: 1. kitchen counter, 2. stair steps, 3. window sills and door thresholds. (If he meant 3 slabs or 3 ft, the calculator below still works: add a line.)
table: Black with gold flecks; hides crumbs and water marks
Plain deep black; shows dust and water spots
notes: Ask for 18–20 mm thickness, a polished and rounded front edge, and a flamed or leather (non-shiny) finish on stair treads so they're not slippery. Seal the kitchen counter every 1–3 years.

tiles.h: Papa's measurement list: what it means
p: Each line is length × width in feet for a floor, or running length × tiling height for walls. Below, each line is read against our measured plan. Edit any number, the tile size or the pieces per box (check the box label); totals add 10% for cutting and breakage and round up to full boxes.
notes: Improvements to the list: (1) add the hall and passage, the biggest area; (2) say which bedroom is 12×19; (3) add the second small bathroom; (4) for walls, subtract doors and windows (a door is about 3 × 7 = 21 sq ft); (5) add skirting; (6) buy all boxes of one tile from the same batch and keep one spare box.
links: How much extra tile to buy

ul: Same batch / shade code on every box of one tile (printed on the box). Different batches differ in colour.
Open 2–3 boxes at the shop: look for chips, warped tiles and size differences.
Big tiles on tile adhesive, not a thick cement bed, with levelling clips and 2–3 mm spacers.
Bathrooms: waterproofing + 24-hour water test first, floor sloped to the drain, epoxy grout.
Tap test with a coin before the final payment: a hollow 'tuk' means air under the tile.
Keep 1 spare box of every tile for future repairs; the same design may not be available later.
